items: HTTP/3 (RFC 9114) is HTTP semantics mapped onto QUIC
Same methods, status codes, headers; different framing, no TCP
QUIC owns streams, reliability, flow control, congestion control
So HTTP/3's own framing layer is far thinner than HTTP/2's
One request/response pair = one QUIC bidirectional stream
HTTP/3 never implements multiplexing itself; it inherits it
Frames: HEADERS, DATA, SETTINGS, GOAWAY, MAX_PUSH_ID
No RST_STREAM (QUIC's RESET_STREAM does it), no WINDOW_UPDATE
Unidirectional streams carry control data, tagged by a type byte
One control stream per side, plus QPACK encoder and decoder streams
HPACK's dynamic table assumes strictly ordered delivery
With QUIC, header blocks can arrive out of order
They would then decode against the wrong table state
QPACK (RFC 9204) fixes this without giving up compression
Static table grows to 99 entries, tuned with modern headers
A dynamic table still exists, per connection
Table updates move onto separate unidirectional encoder/decoder streams
Each header block declares the table state it needs
If that state has not arrived, only that block's decode blocks
A deliberately bounded, per-block HOL risk
`SETTINGS_QPACK_BLOCKED_STREAMS` caps how many streams may block
Set it to 0 and decoding never blocks, at the cost of compression

blocks.title: The Dial To Remember
blocks.text: Maximum compression means referencing the newest table entries; maximum independence means referencing only entries you know arrived. QPACK lets you pick a point between.

items: Base and relative indexing make references position-independent
So an encoder emits blocks without knowing exact decoder progress

lines: # learned over h1.1/h2, used next connection

blocks.title: Fallback Is Built In
items: Happy-Eyeballs-style racing: try QUIC and TCP in parallel
Use whichever completes first
A UDP-blocking network degrades instead of failing
HTTP/3 is TLS 1.3-only; no cleartext, port 443 but over UDP

blocks.text: HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 optimize latency and connection efficiency, not raw throughput. A single large file download barely changes version to version.

items: Corporate proxies that only speak TCP force fallback
Userspace QUIC costs noticeably more CPU per byte
TCP has decades of NIC offload: TSO/LRO, kernel TLS
QUIC's per-packet crypto improves with GSO, but is still heavier
Fast, reliable datacenter link: h2 or even h1.1 keep-alive is fine
gRPC standardized on HTTP/2 for good reason
It needs h2 framing for streaming RPC and trailers
Big JSON responses, few requests: little benefit
Chatty APIs with many parallel small calls: a lot

slides.page_title: When Each Version Helps (and When It Doesn't)

blocks.title: Adoption Is An Edge Toggle
blocks.text: HTTP/3 is usually a CDN or reverse-proxy switch, not an application rewrite. The origin can happily stay on HTTP/1.1 behind it.

blocks.q: Which version should I benchmark with?
a_bullets: Yours, at your real RTT and loss profile
Protocol wins are workload-shaped, not universal
Vendor benchmarks assume conditions you may not have

blocks.title: Where 0-RTT Pays
blocks.text: High-RTT paths make the saved handshake round trip real user-visible time; that is exactly where repeat visits with a stored ticket shine.

items: Keeping sharding, spriting, giant bundles, inlining after enabling h2
Assuming h2 fixed all HOL blocking — it fixed the application layer only
Terminating h2 at the CDN, then proxying to origin over h1.1 with no keep-alive
Sending uppercase header names through an h2 client library
Sending `Connection: keep-alive` over h2 — protocol error, not a warning
Leaving `INITIAL_WINDOW_SIZE` at 64 KB on high-BDP paths, then blaming the network
Treating 0-RTT as free when it is replayable
Believing HTTP/3 needs a new port; it is 443/UDP

blocks.title: The Silent Firewall
blocks.text: A firewall allowing only 443/TCP does not error — it silently forces every client back to HTTP/2, and your h3 rollout shows zero traffic.

items: Measure TTFB and Largest Contentful Paint, not total bytes
Measure them under simulated loss and RTT, not on your office fibre

blocks.text: Clients race the options rather than failing over serially, so users experience slower loads, not error pages.

blocks.title: Security, Three Lines
items: HPACK and QPACK never-indexed literals keep secrets out of tables
QUIC's address validation limits reflection amplification to 3x
Rapid Reset proved cheap stream creation is a DoS surface

blocks.title: The Arc In One Breath
blocks.text: HTTP/2 multiplexed streams onto one TCP connection and compressed headers with HPACK; TCP's ordered byte stream still blocked them, so HTTP/3 rebuilt the transport on UDP as QUIC, moved streams into the transport, integrated TLS 1.3, and adapted compression as QPACK.

blocks.title: What To Actually Ship
blocks.text: HTTP/2 everywhere as the baseline, HTTP/3 at the edge for mobile and lossy users, HTTP/1.1 kept only as a fallback.
